Reducing a model's size

Source: vignettes/articles/model-size.Rmd
model-size.Rmd

Most models worth building are larger than the solver available to them. The usual response is to make the model smaller, and energyRt offers eight ways to do it. They are not interchangeable: each removes something different, and each pays for the saving in a different currency.

Three questions separate them.

What is removed — cells of the calendar, cells of the geoscale, milestone years, or merely the freedom to decide. Whether any value is recomputed — a reduction that only drops rows leaves every remaining number exactly as declared, while one that merges cells must combine values, and combining them is where meaning can be lost. Whether the answer is still the full model’s — two of the eight reductions are exact, five approximate, and three of the approximations report their own error.

This article treats each reduction in the same six terms. A companion article, vignette("resolution"), maps the same ground by axis rather than by cost, and vignette("time-resolution") and vignette("space-resolution") cover one axis each in depth.

library(energyRt)
open_project(tempdir())   # every driver below writes scenarios to a project

topia_elc <- topia$modules$electricity   # twelve regions, five zones
mod <- newModel("TOPIA", data = topia_elc$repo,
                calendar = calendars[["d365_h24_1dpm"]],
                region   = topia_elc$regions,
                horizon  = topia$modules$horizons$BY2025_50_by10,
                discount = 0.05)
mod <- setGeoscale(mod, topia_elc$geoscale)

Time

Calendar sampling

  • Reduces the number of timeslices, by drawing whole members of one level (days, weeks, seasons) and keeping every finer slice beneath them. A year of 8760 hours solved on twelve sampled days carries 288.
  • Recomputes nothing. A sample is a label-subset of the full calendar: timeslice names, levels and shares are the originals. What changes is pTimesliceWeight, which carries 1 / year_fraction, so twelve days weigh 30.4167 each and the sample annualises exactly. Parameter rows outside the sample are dropped, not averaged.
  • Size falls in proportion to the slices kept, in every timeslice-indexed row and column: dispatch, storage levels, flows, availability factors.
  • The answer estimates the full year. Each sample is a replicate, not a shard, so sample objectives form a distribution and must never be summed — the opposite of solving by region. Sampling smooths extremes, so peaking capacity and storage are the quantities that suffer first. A sample must retain at least two members at every level below the year: dropping a level renames the leaf timeslices, the model’s data stops matching, and the result solves to zero without complaint.
  • Used for screening, parameter sweeps, and questions where the spread of answers is more informative than one answer.
  • Driven by calendar_samples(), which writes the draw as an editable table, and solve_by_sample(), which solves each sample as an own-problem variant of one scenario. sample_summary() reads the distribution back.
cal <- calendars[["d365_h24"]]

# consecutive blocks tiling the year: the deterministic, full-coverage crawl
sam <- calendar_samples(cal, n = 2, seed = 1)

# or two random draws of two seasons each, without replacement: the draws are
# disjoint, so n x sample_size cannot exceed the level's membership
calendar_samples(cal, level = "SEASON", sample_size = 2, n = 2,
                 method = "random", seed = 42)

smp <- solve_by_sample(mod, name = "BY_SAMPLE", samples = sam,
                       solver = solver_options$glpk)

# the spread of installed capacity across the replicates
sample_summary(smp, "vTechCap", by = "tech")

Three traversals are offered. "sequential" tiles the year in consecutive blocks and covers it completely; "random" draws disjoint samples without replacement, so coverage may be partial; "bootstrap" draws with replacement, and a member drawn twice becomes a scaled share rather than a repeated row, because a calendar holds each timeslice once.

Calendar coarsening

  • Reduces the number of timeslices by moving the model onto a coarser calendar — hours into days, days into seasons — rather than by selecting from the fine one.
  • Recomputes every timeslice-indexed value. Each column moves by its declared rule: extensive quantities add, intensive ones take a weighted mean, and a column with no merged form is reported rather than invented. Rules can be overridden per column.
  • Size falls with the coarse calendar’s cardinality, and unlike sampling it falls for the whole year at once rather than for a drawn part of it.
  • The answer loses the variation inside each coarse slice, and no reweighting recovers it. One deterministic result rather than a distribution: there is no sampling error, because the error is the averaging. A recast model is its own model, and comparing its objective against the fine model’s compares two models rather than measuring an error.
  • Used for a model that must stay cheap permanently, and as the cheap intermediate stage of a guided solve.
  • Driven by recast_model_calendar(), over timescales::recast_calendar().
annual <- recast_model_calendar(mod, topia$modules$calendars$annual)

# monthly hours, with one column moved by a rule other than its declared one
monthly <- recast_model_calendar(mod, topia$modules$calendars$m12_h24,
                                 rules = c(demand = "sum"))

A given base year

  • Reduces the year axis. The milestones before the base year are history and enter no linear programme at all; the base year is solved on its own; the projection optimises what remains.
  • Recomputes nothing. What the base year decided crosses into the projection as stock — exogenous, sunk, paying no annualised capital charge — leaving the model’s declared @stock untouched. Every departed year still anchors interpolation, because the interpolation grid already includes anchor years outside the solved set.
  • Size falls by the removed years’ full share of the problem, which on a long horizon with history is the largest single reduction available.
  • The answer is exact for the projection, conditional on accepting the base-year result. Nothing about the remaining years is approximated, which makes this a reduction rather than an approximation.
  • Used for calibrated runs, where the base year is a measurement rather than a decision.
  • Driven by newHorizon(base_year = ), solve_base_year() and interpolate_model(base_year_scenario = ).
# the horizon `mod` already carries: 2025 given, then 2030/2040/2050 decided
newHorizon(period = 2025:2055, intervals = c(1, 10, 10, 10), base_year = 2025)

by  <- solve_base_year(mod, solver = solver_options$glpk)
prj <- interpolate_model(mod, name = "PROJECTION", base_year_scenario = by)

The split is made by slicing the interval table rather than by flagging a year inside it. Every derived set — the first and next milestone, the investment and stock windows, the stock path — reads intervals$mid or sets$year, so a slice moves them together, while a flag would leave a set naming a year the problem does not contain.

Horizon windows

  • Reduces the number of years in any one solve. The horizon is sliced into consecutive windows, each deciding step milestones, with overlap further milestones appended as look-ahead whose decisions are discarded.
  • Recomputes nothing. Each window re-interpolates the pristine model with the accumulated ledger applied, so no window inherits another’s rounding.
  • Size falls to roughly one window’s share, and the sequence is many small problems in place of one large one.
  • The answer loses perfect foresight and is sub-optimal by construction. Its objective is not comparable with a full-horizon one: capacity carried as stock pays no annualised charge, so comparing the two numbers measures an accounting difference as much as a foresight penalty.
  • Used for horizons that do not fit whole, and for representing agents who genuinely cannot see ahead.
  • Driven by horizon_windows() and solve_recursive().
# what the sequence will decide, before committing to it
vapply(horizon_windows(getHorizon(mod), step = 2L, overlap = 1L),
       function(w) w$horizon@name, character(1))

seq_res <- solve_recursive(mod, step = 2L, overlap = 1L,
                           solver = solver_options$glpk)

Space

Region subsetting

  • Reduces the region set to a sub-territory, keeping the model’s own resolution in what remains.
  • Recomputes nothing. Rows outside the kept regions are dropped. A trade route with one endpoint outside the set becomes a boundary stub — an import or an export at the price the severed neighbour would have traded at — or, with no price, is dropped, which makes the sub-model an island and generally understates its options.
  • Size falls with the share of regions kept, in every region-indexed row and column.
  • The answer is exact when nothing crosses the boundary. Regional quantities are extensive, so sub-problems solved without trade have objectives that sum to the full model’s. Once a boundary price is supplied, each piece faces an exterior the others cannot see and the objectives are no longer additive; the result records which case applied. A cost declared at a coarser level does not scale with a subset, and is warned about before the surgery rather than after.
  • Used for single-country studies inside a continental dataset, and as the shard of a spatial decomposition.
  • Driven by subset_model_regions(), by interpolate_model() when handed a filtered geoscale, and by solve_by_region() with its three boundary modes. boundary_window() sizes the stub from the region’s own demand.
west <- subset_model_regions(mod, region = c("R02", "R03"))   # zone Z2

# the same cut, but facing an exterior rather than an edge: a stepped curve
# around a supplied price, sized from the severed routes' own demand
bw   <- boundary_window(mod, regions = c("R02", "R03"), price = 60, nsteps = 3)
west <- subset_model_regions(mod, region = c("R02", "R03"), boundary_prices = bw)

# or let the driver cut, solve and store each region in turn
by_reg <- solve_by_region(mod, trade = "none", solver = solver_options$glpk)

boundary_window() derives the quantity a stub may carry and will not invent its price: a price must be supplied, because the number that belongs there is the neighbour’s marginal value of the commodity, which only a solved model knows.

Region aggregation

  • Reduces the region set by rolling the model up to a coarser geoframe — sites into zones, zones into countries.
  • Recomputes every region-indexed value. Extensive quantities add, intensive ones take a mean weighted by the size of each contributing region, and corridors merge only when they agree on commodity and cluster structure. A value with no merged form — a lifetime, a levy rate — stops the call and names the object, the column and the regions that disagree, unless resolve_conflicts is set to take their mean or to leave the value unset.
  • Size falls with the coarse region count, and with it the intra-zone network: routes inside a merged region cease to exist.
  • The answer bounds the fine one in neither direction. With uniform efficiency across the merged regions the coarse objective is lower, because merging removed transport limits; with heterogeneous efficiency it is higher, because averaging destroyed the ability to dispatch the best unit first. What is lost is the difference between a zone’s cheap sites and its dear ones, and a model that cannot see that difference builds the average everywhere.
  • Used for continental models in which only aggregate behaviour is asked of most regions.
  • Driven by aggregate_model_regions(), which returns a model declared over the coarser regions and carrying the pruned geoscale.
repo <- newRepository(
  "mini",
  newCommodity("COA", unit = "MMBtu"),
  newCommodity("ELC", unit = "MWh", timeframe = "ANNUAL"),
  newSupply("SUP_COA", commodity = "COA", supply = data.frame(cost = 1)),
  newTechnology("ECOA", input = list(comm = "COA"), output = list(comm = "ELC"),
                cap2act = 1, invcost = list(invcost = 100),
                olife = list(olife = 30)),
  newDemand("DEM", commodity = "ELC",
            demand = data.frame(region = c("R02", "R03"), year = 2020,
                                demand = 10))
)
mini <- newModel("MINI", data = repo, calendar = calendars$annual,
                 region = c("R02", "R03"), horizon = horizons$Y2020_2060_by_5)

# the two regions roll up into the zone they share
zones <- aggregate_model_regions(mini, geoscale = topia$geoscales$squares,
                                 level = "zone")
get_region(zones)

Clusters within an aggregation

  • Reduces less, deliberately. The fine regions inside each coarse region are grouped into k connected clusters, carried as parallel sub-processes with their own capacity, availability and costs.
  • Recomputes within each cluster instead of within each coarse region.
  • Size sits between the two extremes and is tunable: k runs from one cluster per coarse region — exactly plain aggregation — up to one per fine region, which averages nothing.
  • The answer recovers the part of the spread that matters. At the upper end of k, a model whose fine regions already pool inside each coarse region reproduces the fine objective exactly. Settings are per technology family, because one k for a whole model is meaningless: a coal fleet groups on cost and efficiency, a wind fleet on resource quality and profile shape. Clusters never straddle a coarse region, and a family that already has clusters keeps them — the two groupings compose.
  • Used for keeping resource heterogeneity in an otherwise coarse model, which is the usual reason an aggregated renewables model misbehaves.
  • Driven by aggregate_model_regions(clusters = ), with get_process_groups() to see what can be merged and process_cluster_sweep() to see where the structure is. The grouping is a scale-construction method supplied by nestedscales, and the number of clusters is reported rather than chosen: k = "auto" picks the best average silhouette, which is a rule and not an answer.
get_process_groups(mod)        # what could be merged, and over which regions

# per family, never one k for the model:
# aggregate_model_regions(mod, level = "zone",
#                         clusters = list(ECOA = list(k = 3,
#                                                     features = c("invcost",
#                                                                  "eff")),
#                                         EWIN = 8))

A full worked example, with objectives at every k from plain aggregation to the fine model, is in vignette("region-aggregation").

Fixing decisions rather than removing cells

The reductions above make a model smaller. The two below leave its dimensions untouched and remove freedom instead, and they are what turn the reductions into methods: a cheap solve answers a question, and its answer constrains the expensive one.

Carried stock

  • Reduces the free investment decisions. Capacity decided by an earlier solve re-enters a later one as exogenous stock at its true vintage.
  • Recomputes nothing; the model’s own declared @stock is left alone and the carried fleet is added at the vintage it was built.
  • Size: the same rows, materially fewer free columns, and a much easier problem.
  • The answer treats the carried fleet as sunk — it pays no annualised capital charge. That is what a past decision should cost, and it is also why objectives along such a sequence are not comparable with a single full-horizon objective.
  • Used by sequential solving, where each window inherits what its predecessors decided.
  • Driven by solution_ledger(), which reads a solved scenario into a ledger, and internally by solve_recursive() and solve_guided(), which apply it. Carrying stock is a property of those drivers rather than a step to be performed by hand.

Capacity targets

  • Reduces the search space, by turning a cheap solve’s answer into bounds on an expensive one: cap.lo, or fixed, with optional slack.
  • Recomputes nothing. Targets are written into the model’s own bound columns and re-interpolated; no solver variable is fixed behind the model’s back.
  • Size: unchanged in rows and columns, far smaller in search.
  • The answer still pays for everything it builds, so the guided solve remains an ordinary one and its objective is comparable with a true perfect-foresight objective. The comparison has a known sign — guided is never better than perfect foresight — and the gap is the price of the guidance.
  • Used for full-horizon problems that are intractable head-on but tractable once told roughly where to arrive.
  • Driven by solution_targets() and apply_targets(), and by solve_guided(), which sequences the cheap solves: an optional base year, an end state, an optional cheap transition on a reduced calendar, each interior milestone refined against the end state, and finally one full-horizon solve carrying the accumulated bounds. guided_gap() reports the price.
gdd <- solve_guided(mod, stages = c("endpoint", "pairs", "final"),
                    slack = 0.2, mode = "lo",
                    calendar_guide = topia$modules$calendars$annual,
                    solver = solver_options$glpk)

# What the guidance cost. Only measurable where the full problem is solvable
# both ways, which is how the method is validated before it is relied on.
scen_pf <- mod |>
  interpolate_model(name = "PF") |>
  solve_scenario(solver = solver_options$glpk)

guided_gap(gdd, pf = scen_pf)

What distinguishes this from sequential solving is that every subproblem still sees where it has to arrive. Targets build and pay; carried stock is sunk and does not — the distinction is why the two are separate primitives.

Reductions that change nothing

interpolate_model(fold = , sparse = , prune = ), the rule-defined mapping sets and trim_parameters() make a model cheaper to build, store and solve without removing a single modelling cell. The answer is identical by construction; options(energyRt.map_rules_verify = TRUE) checks each rule against the table it replaces. These are representation choices, not resolution choices.

scen <- interpolate_model(mod, name = "COMPACT", fold = TRUE, sparse = TRUE)
model_size(scen)

model_size() is also the way to find out what any of the earlier reductions actually achieved, rather than what it was expected to achieve.

Choosing

The question being asked The reduction that fits
Is the base year measured rather than decided? a given base year — exact, and usually the largest single win
Does the question concern a few regions? region subsetting — exact when nothing crosses the boundary
Does the answer hinge on intra-annual detail? coarsen the calendar, or sample it and report the spread
Does it hinge on resource quality? aggregate with clusters, never plainly
Is the full horizon simply too large? guided solving, whose gap is measurable; sequential only where foresight is genuinely absent
Is the model merely slow to build or store? fold, sparse, prune, trim_parameters()

Two reductions are exact: a given base year, and a region subset whose boundary is severed. The rest approximate, and three of them say by how much: sample_summary() for the sampling spread, guided_gap() for the guidance penalty, and each object’s @misc$aggregation record for what was merged, forced or dropped on the way up.

The approximations also compose, which is how large models are usually made solvable: a sampled calendar on an aggregated geoscale, solved region by region, is four of these features at once. Composing them multiplies the saving and compounds the error, and nothing in the framework warns about the combination — only about each part.

What is not yet possible

Three things a reader may reasonably expect are not implemented, and are named here so the boundary is explicit rather than implied.

Uneven resolution across space. Resolution is a property of the model, not of the cell: aggregate_model_regions(level = ) moves the whole model to one level. A model fine in two regions and coarse in the remaining forty-eight cannot yet be declared, although the refusals that stand in the way are all stated and none is fundamental.

Uneven resolution across time. One calendar serves every milestone year. A pathway with 8760 hours in 2030, 2040 and 2050 and a twelve-day sample in 2035 and 2045 cannot yet be declared.

A boundary price taken from a solved model. boundary_window() sizes a stub’s quantity but refuses to invent its price, and nothing derives that price from a neighbour’s solution, because the right number is a dual of the commodity balance.

And one thing that is refused by design rather than unbuilt: no reduction runs backwards. The balance layer aggregates and never disaggregates, so no operation takes a solved coarse result and distributes it over finer regions or slices. Disaggregation means building a finer model and solving it.
